title: Research Bits: Aug. 18
gist: Three academic research results in neuromorphic and edge-AI hardware: a memristive analog in-memory computing platform using hyperdimensional computing for edge NLP, a programmable dynamic memtransistor with tunable response speeds for time-series AI, and a surface-acoustic-wave-controlled artificial synapse with independent long- and short-term memory.

insights.claim: Researchers from UMass Amherst and TetraMem combined memristive analog in-memory computing hardware with hyperdimensional computing algorithms and achieved 95.24% accuracy in a language-identification proof of concept.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Analog in-memory NLP points to far lower-energy edge inference, relevant to on-device AI silicon roadmaps.
insights.quote: their system achieved 95.24% accuracy in language identification.

insights.claim: The approach turns the intrinsic randomness of memristive devices—usually considered a drawback—into a feature for the encoding step, and is expected to extend from written to spoken language processing on edge devices.
insights.speaker: Qiangfei Xia
insights.so_what: Reframing device non-ideality as usable entropy could ease manufacturability of analog AI chips.
insights.quote: The encoding part leverages the intrinsic randomness of memristive devices, considered by many to be a drawback for this device technology
insights.locator: Xia quote, UMass Riccio College of Engineering

insights.claim: KAIST designed a programmable dynamic memtransistor (PDM) with a dual-layer structure whose electron-trapping layer tunes recovery speed nonvolatilely, reducing prediction errors by up to 40 times for time-varying data versus fixed-response devices.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Programmable temporal response targets real-time AI in autonomous vehicles, robots and wearables at lower power.
insights.quote: it reduced prediction errors by up to 40 times for time-varying data.

insights.claim: The KAIST device tuned current-recovery time over roughly a 5-fold range and characteristic frequency over more than a 10-fold range, enabling one semiconductor to process data changing at different speeds.
insights.speaker: Shinhyun Choi
insights.so_what: Adaptive-speed processing in a single device could reduce power and part count in edge AI systems.
insights.quote: This study demonstrates an AI semiconductor whose response characteristics can be programmed to efficiently process data changing at different speeds
insights.locator: Choi quote, KAIST School of Electrical Engineering

insights.claim: Researchers from Sungkyunkwan, Ajou, University of Tokyo and Hanyang developed a neuromorphic device integrating a monolayer MoS2 memristor and a surface-acoustic-wave device to independently implement long-term (electrical) and short-term (SAW-controlled) memory.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Independently controllable synaptic memory advances reservoir-computing hardware for low-power pattern recognition.
insights.locator: Artificial synapse with long- and short-term memory

insights.claim: The reconfigurable synapse maintained stable operation beyond 10,000 seconds of repeated operation and reached 96.1% recognition accuracy on a character-classification task using reservoir computing.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Demonstrated endurance and accuracy move SAW-based neuromorphic devices toward practical viability.
insights.quote: achieved a recognition accuracy of 96.1% in a character classification task when applied to reservoir computing.
